articles.title: Go inside the $10.2 million Iowa mansion getting national attention
articles.summary: What does $10.2 million get you in Iowa? Castle Lake Manor includes 5 bedrooms, nearly 80 acres of woodland and international artifacts throughout.
articles.body:
A mansion in Toddville, just listed for $10.2 million , making it the most expensive home for sale in Iowa. That price tag includes nearly 80 acres of private woodland in rural Linn County, a giant lake right next to the house and — perhaps the most interesting part of it all — international artifacts woven into the mansion itself.

The original owners, the Christophersons, spent years traveling around the globe sourcing decorations and materials for the home they dubbed Castle Lake Manor. There's a Louis XV marble mantel sourced from Montreux, Switzerland, made around 1875. Another is a carved verde marble Rococo mantel from Paris. There's stained glass from Uruguay.

And for the pub in the lower level? It's hand-carved mahogany, transported from Sheffield, England.

This 'European estate' in Iowa listed for $10.2 million. See inside.

Castle Lake Manor already looks impressive from the photos. But when real estate agent Holly Lovell stepped into it for the first time, she was "completely mesmerized."

The Christophersons "really just had a spectacular taste in history and design and European flair," Lovell said. "There's so much love put into this."

The previous record for the most expensive home in Iowa was a $9.5 million home sitting on the Okoboji lakefront . That house was also sold by Lovell in 2024.

articles.title: Who is Ben Delo? British crypto billionaire pardoned by Trump donates £36m to Reform UK
articles.summary: UK News: Ben Delo, a British crypto entrepreneur and BitMEX co-founder, pledges £36 million to Reform UK, marking the largest political donation in British history. Discover more about Delo's impact and his views on the future of UK politics.
articles.body: British crypto investor Ben Delo has pledged £36 million ($48.7) to Reform UK, giving Nigel Farage’s party its biggest political donation as it prepares for a possible run at government.Delo, co-founder of cryptocurrency trading platform BitMEX, said he would provide £1 million a month until the next UK general election, expected by mid-2029. He said the funding would help Reform prepare for government and compete with Labour and the Conservatives.The donation is the largest single contribution recorded for a British political party, according to the Electoral Commission’s database. It is more than three times the £10 million previously donated to the Conservatives by businessman John Sainsbury, who died in 2022.Delo has already donated £8 million to Reform and has been a long-standing supporter of the party. The British crypto entrepreneur was convicted in the United States of violating the Bank Secrecy Act and was later pardoned by US President Donald Trump, Reuters reported.In an opinion article published by The Telegraph, Delo said his experience of running a startup under intense scrutiny had influenced his decision to continue backing Reform.He argued that the party should focus less on fundraising and put more resources into developing policies and preparing legislation ahead of a potential return to government.“Reform are making serious plans for the government,” Delo wrote, arguing that creating detailed policies and legislation requires both time and money.The announcement comes as Reform faces questions over allegations surrounding political donations. The party's support in opinion polls has also fallen after maintaining a strong lead for much of the past year.An undercover investigation earlier this month alleged that two senior Reform aides arranged for a foreign donor to fund political polling. Police are investigating the allegations, while Farage suspended the two aides following the claims.Delo did not directly address that investigation in his article.Farage welcomed the new funding, saying he was “honoured and humbled” by Delo’s confidence in Reform. He said the party was the only political force capable of reversing what he described as Britain’s decline.Delo said he recognised the risks faced by people financially supporting Reform while the party remains under scrutiny.“Right now it takes a thick skin to back Reform financially,” he wrote, questioning whether successful businesspeople would be willing to publicly associate themselves with the party because of concerns about their reputation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Australian researchers recover almost 100% of silver from solar-cell waste, helping Australia tackle 1 million tonnes of retired panels by 2050
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australia could be sitting on a hidden stockpile of hundreds of tonnes of silver as millions of solar panels approach the end of their working lives. .
articles.body: Australia could be sitting on a hidden stockpile of hundreds of tonnes of silver as millions of solar panels approach the end of their working lives. More than one million tonnes of waste solar panels are expected across the country by 2050, containing an estimated 300–500 tonnes of silver. Much of that valuable metal is currently left behind when panels are discarded. Now, researchers at the University of Newcastle have demonstrated a continuous flotation process that recovered almost 100 per cent of silver from end-of-life solar-cell material. The breakthrough could help make solar-panel recycling more commercially viable while keeping valuable resources out of landfill.Australia expects 1 million tonnes of solar waste by 2050The scale of Australia’s future solar-panel waste is central to the problem. According to the University of Newcastle, more than one million tonnes of waste panels are expected in Australia by 2050, with those panels estimated to contain 300–500 tonnes of silver.That creates a situation in which a large quantity of a valuable metal could end up being treated as waste. The university notes that glass and aluminium are already routinely recovered from discarded panels, but silver is often left within the solar-cell material. Associate Professor Mahshid Firouzi put the problem bluntly: “We're effectively burying silver in landfill when we can recover it and return it to the economy.”Researchers use flotation to recover silverResearchers at the University of Newcastle have been developing froth flotation as a way to separate silver from end-of-life solar cells. The technique is widely used in mineral processing and works by helping the silver attach to air bubbles, allowing it to be separated from the rest of the material. Unlike conventional approaches that rely heavily on acid, the Newcastle process uses water, air and small amounts of chemicals.The researchers moved beyond small laboratory-style batch testing and demonstrated continuous operation. According to the study published in a ChemRxiv preprint, titled ‘Continuous flotation unlocks full recovery of silver from end-of-life solar cells’, the researchers processed about 22 kilograms of solar-cell material, corresponding to roughly 468 kilograms of rooftop photovoltaic panels. During continuous operation lasting around 90 minutes, silver recovery remained close to 100 per cent, while the steady-state testing produced an average silver upgrade of approximately 83-fold.Pilot recovers almost 100% of silverThe University of Newcastle reported that the pilot recovered almost 100 per cent of the silver and concentrated it into a high-value product representing only 1.25 per cent of the original material. The resulting product contained more than 80 times the silver concentration of the starting solar-cell material.Researchers are also looking at whether the process can operate continuously and at a scale that could eventually support commercial recycling. Associate Professor Firouzi said the latest work showed that flotation could operate continuously at a much larger scale with nearly 100 per cent silver recovery, bringing the technology closer to commercial implementation.Solar-panel recycling costs $10–$15 per panelOne of the biggest barriers to recycling solar panels is cost. The University of Newcastle estimates that recycling currently costs around $10 to $15 per panel, while sending a panel to landfill can cost only a few dollars. Recovering silver could provide an additional source of value that helps narrow that gap.The flotation process could be three to five times less expensive than conventional acid-leaching methods. According to the university, acid-based approaches can be costly to scale because they require large quantities of chemicals and create hazardous waste that must be managed. “Silver is the highest-value material in a solar cell,” Firouzi said, arguing that recovering it could make solar-panel recycling considerably more financially attractive.Even so, the continuous pilot-scale results point towards a potentially important role for resource recovery as Australia’s current generation of solar panels eventually reaches the end of its working life. The university says the team is also investigating whether the technology could be applied to other waste streams, including printed circuit boards and electronic waste.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, al-Qaida and terror camps have returned to Afghanistan: US
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: Al-Qaida and terrorist training camps are back in Afghanistan 25 years after 9/11.The terrorist organisation and it.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Al-Qaida and terrorist training camps are back in Afghanistan 25 years after 9/11.The terrorist organisation and its affiliates have established at least eight training sites in Afghanistan over the past three years, exploiting the security vacuum created by the Taliban’s return to power and the US withdrawal in 2021, the Washington Post reported on Saturday.UN monitors and Western intelligence officials say the camps are being used for weapons, explosives, guerrilla warfare and increasingly sophisticated instruction involving encryption, drones and artificial intelligence.Core al-Qaida now numbers perhaps 100 fighters and is functioning less as an expeditionary army than as a "consulting service" for other militants. Other terror groups, including an affiliate of the Islamic State, al-Qaida’s main rival, also have set up new training sites, giving “militant Islamist groups” a foothold in at least 14 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, the report said.For New Delhi, the most unsettling part of the Post’s wake-up call on al-Qaida’s revival is not that the terror group is rebuilding training camps; it is that the geography, networks and regional ecosystem surrounding those camps look hauntingly familiar.India endured terrorist violence throughout the 1990s and 2000s while the American public was only beginning to wake up to the transnational jihadist threat, so this is less a new chapter than an old warning with updated technology because the al-Qaida story is deeply intertwined with Pakistan.The 9/11 Commission documented how Ramzi Yousef, mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, met Khalid Sheikh Mohammed in Pakistan and was eventually captured in Islamabad in 1995. KSM – a Pakistani national mistakenly described as Kuwaiti because he was born there – himself lived in Pakistan before moving to Afghanistan, where he met Osama bin Laden and presented the idea that became the 9/11 operation. He remains imprisoned in Guantanamo.Other senior al-Qaida figures followed similar trajectories. Abu Zubaydah was captured in Pakistan in 2002 as was Ramzi bin al-Shibh; KSM was captured in Rawalpindi the following year. And bin Laden himself, the man who had spent years as the world's most wanted terrorist, was finally found not in some inaccessible Afghan cave but in Abbottabad, Pakistan, less than two miles from the country's premier military academy. US forces killed him there in May 2011.That history gives Indian analysts pause when Washington's gaze once again settles overwhelmingly on Afghanistan — and, unsurprisingly now, Iran -- because the US typically takes a more benign view of client states such as Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. The Post reports that al-Qaida's current leader, Egyptian Saif al-Adel, is believed to be hiding in Iran.New Delhi has often questioned why Pakistan's role in the movement's historical infrastructure so often receives less sustained scrutiny; Afghanistan is landlocked, but it is not hermetically sealed. It borders Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and China. Historically, however, Pakistan has been the principal southern gateway connecting Afghanistan to the Arabian Sea and the wider world. Peshawar, Karachi and the tribal belt repeatedly figured in the logistics of the Afghan jihad and later transnational militancy.While this does not make Pakistan responsible for every terrorist who passed through it, it does, however, make Pakistan a key part of the story. The 1993 Bombay bombings, the 2001 attack on Parliament and, later, the 2008 Mumbai attacks were part of a long continuum of terrorism in South Asia.The Indian government has repeatedly described Pakistan-based militant organizations with ties to a wider "jihad" as a central component of that threat. The 26/11 attackers, for example, departed from Karachi, hijacked an Indian fishing vessel and sailed to Mumbai to carry out one of the bloodiest terrorist attacks in history. US authorities subsequently described LET as responsible for the attacks but have moved at a snail’s pace in helping bring the masterminds of the attack to justice.While the LeT itself was established in Afghanistan's Kunar province in 1986, it subsequently focused its attention on India. Abu Zubaydah, a senior al-Qaida operative, was captured at an LeT safehouse in Faisalabad, demonstrating that the two networks could overlap operationally.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: BRICS Summit: Xi calls for greater commitment to Middle East peace
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on BRICS member states to do more to promote peace in the Middle East and the Gulf region. Speaking at the BRICS summ...
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping calls for greater commitment to promoting peace in the Middle East and Gulf region at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi.

Xi Jinping emphasizes the need for BRICS nations to address power politics, international order challenges, and peace and security shortcomings in the region.

China is set to take over the BRICS chairmanship next year, with President Xi Jinping making diplomatic efforts including visits to India, Kyrgyzstan, and Egypt.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on BRICS member states to do more to promote peace in the Middle East and the Gulf region.

Speaking at the BRICS summit in New Delhi on Saturday, he said that China was prepared to play its part, alongside the other members of the grouping, in establishing peace and stability.

The situation in the region is complex, and the war is inflicting heavy losses on the peoples of the region, the Chinese leader said.

Xi also pointed out that power politics are on the rise, the international order is being challenged and there are growing shortcomings in terms of peace and security. The BRICS nations must stand "on the right side of history," he urged.

The acronym BRICS stands for the first letters of the group's first five members: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. Saudi Arabia, Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Indonesia are also members. The group also sees itself as a counterweight to the West. China will take over the BRICS chairmanship next year.

Xi travelled to India for the first time since 2019, and held a bilateral meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Relations between the world's two most populous countries deteriorated significantly following a fatal incident in 2020 involving soldiers from both sides on the shared border in a disputed area of the Himalayas. Relations have improved somewhat since an agreement in 2024.

The trip to New Delhi is part of a series of recent diplomatic efforts by Xi, with visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.

articles.title: Germany suspects Russian spy link in Leipzig airport drone plot: Report
articles.summary: Europe News: A suspected explosive-laden drone discovered at Leipzig airport last month has led German security officials to investigate possible Russian military .
articles.body: A suspected explosive-laden drone discovered at Leipzig airport last month has led German security officials to investigate possible Russian military intelligence involvement. A report has identified a GRU-linked Russian national as the alleged coordinator of the operation.The drone was discovered on August 4 in a secured cargo area at Leipzig airport, close to a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. German investigators suspect the incident may have been part of a wider “hybrid attack”, according to a report by Welt am Sonntag.The newspaper reported that German authorities believe Russian national Oleg Le, allegedly linked to Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency, acted as the logistics coordinator for the suspected operation. Investigators have also identified a second suspect, Belarusian national Andrei Ka, the report said.The August 4 incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport involved an explosives-laden drone found near a Ukrainian transport jet. German authorities were able to disarm the drone and later the German government officially blamed Russia in early September.The reported findings were cited as the basis for Berlin’s decision to hold Russia responsible for the incident and announce measures targeting Russian diplomatic and cultural facilities in Germany, including the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.According to Welt am Sonntag, investigators believe Le entered Germany from Turkey before travelling onwards to Serbia via Berlin airport. He is now believed to have returned to Russia.The report said German authorities were aware of Le’s alleged links to the GRU when he entered the country but did not place him under surveillance.Investigators reportedly identified the two suspects through DNA traces recovered at Leipzig airport. They are also examining how the explosives may have entered Germany, with the newspaper reporting that the material could have been concealed in trucks travelling through Bulgaria and Serbia.The suspected device was discovered late on August 4 in a secured cargo area at Leipzig airport, close to a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. The airport is a key hub for the movement of military-related goods.Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, declined to comment on the report. An agency spokeswoman told AFP that she could not comment “due to the ongoing investigation”.The reported case comes amid heightened German concerns over suspected Russian-linked sabotage, cyberattacks and other forms of “hybrid” activity. articles.title: Gujarat earthquake, Nepal floods & more: What is it about the date 26?
articles.summary: India News: Gujarat, the tsunami, 26/11, and now Nepal. Some of the disasters etched deepest into public memory have one oddly specific thing in common: they happ.
articles.body: Gujarat, the tsunami, 26/11, and now Nepal. Some of the disasters etched deepest into public memory have one oddly specific thing in common: they happened on the 26th.The coincidence surfaced again after the August 26 catastrophe in Nepal, where a glacier collapse unleashed a wall of mud, rock and water through the Himalayan valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving thousands missing. As images of the destruction spread, so did an old question: what is it about the 26th?But is the date really unusually deadly, or are we simply very good at finding patterns once we know where to look?When nature struck on the 26thThe natural disasters alone would be enough to build a legend around this date. The Gujarat earthquake of January 26, 2001, Republic Day, struck Kutch with such force that it killed close to 20,000 people and injured more than 160,000, flattening entire towns like Bhuj and Anjar. Three years later, on December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent a tsunami crashing into the coastlines of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, part of a disaster that killed or left missing roughly 228,000 people across the Indian Ocean rim. The following July, on July 26, 2005, Mumbai received close to 944 mm of rainfall in 24 hours, a deluge that killed more than a thousand people across Maharashtra and brought the city to a standstill for days.The pattern isn't confined to Indian soil, or even to this century. Turkey's Erzincan earthquake killed an estimated 32,700 people on December 26, 1939. The Skopje earthquake of July 26, 1963 killed around 1,070 and left 200,000 homeless. Iran's Bam earthquake, which levelled a 2,000-year-old citadel city, struck on December 26, 2003, killing roughly 31,000 people. Indonesia's Yogyakarta earthquake killed more than 5,700 on May 26, 2006, and the Hindu Kush earthquake of October 26, 2015 shook Afghanistan, Pakistan and parts of northern India simultaneously.When the 26th turned man-madeWhere the 26th gets stranger is that it isn't only earthquakes and floods, events with no human author. It has also coincided with some of the worst disasters humans have caused deliberately or through negligence.The most seared into Indian memory is November 26, 2008, when ten Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, laying siege to the city for nearly three days and killing 166 people. It is remembered simply as 26/11, a date that needs no year attached to be understood. It wasn't an isolated instance of terrorism landing on this date, either, the Ahmedabad serial blasts of July 26, 2008, one of the deadliest terror strikes on Indian soil that year, fell on the same date. Outside India, the Kabul airport bombing of August 26, 2021, carried out during the US-led evacuation from Afghanistan, killed at least 183 people, including 13 American service members.Industrial and nuclear disasters share the date too, and this is where the list stops looking like a coincidence confined to any one country or cause. Reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded during a botched safety test on April 26, 1986, in what remains the worst nuclear accident in history. More than four decades earlier, on April 26, 1942, a gas and coal-dust explosion at China's Benxihu colliery killed 1,549 miners through carbon monoxide poisoning, one of the deadliest mining disasters ever recorded.Crashes, collisions and the 26thThen there is a third category that rarely makes it into casual conversations about the 26th, but rounds out just how wide its reach is: ordinary transport disasters, the kind that don't need an earthquake or a bomb, just a broken rail or a failed engine part.India's Khanna rail disaster, a derailment and collision caused by a broken rail near Punjab's Khanna town, killed 212 people on November 26, 1998. The Aurangabad air crash, when flight IC-491 went down while approaching the Maharashtra airport, killed 55 of 118 people aboard on April 26, 1993. Overseas, Lauda Air Flight 004 crashed in Thailand on May 26, 1991, after an uncommanded thrust-reverser deployment sent the Boeing 767 out of control, killing all 223 people aboard.Laid end to end, the list stops looking like a curated coincidence and starts looking almost deliberately comprehensive — quakes, tsunamis, floods, terror attacks, a nuclear meltdown, a mine explosion, a rail crash, an air crash. Nearly every disaster category a newsroom covers has, at some point, chosen the 26th.So, is the 26th actually cursed?There's a statistical explanation for this, and it's less exciting than a curse. The British statistician David Hand has spent years studying coincidences like this, he calls it the law of truly large numbers. Basically, if disasters are happening somewhere in the world almost every day, and a month only has 28 to 31 possible dates, some date was bound to end up looking busier than the rest. It just happened to be the 26th. It could as easily have been the 9th.Then there's confirmation bias, which does a lot of the heavy lifting here. Once you start looking for disasters on the 26th, you notice every one that fits and forget the ones that don't. Bhopal's gas leak, India's worst industrial disaster, happened on the night of December 2-3, 1984. The Uttarakhand floods were in June 2013. The Balasore train collision that killed nearly 300 people was on June 2, 2023. None of these are anywhere near the 26th. Nobody brings them up when the "jinx" comes up, because once you believe a pattern, you stop counting the exceptions.Numerology adds a third layer, and in India this one actually sticks with people. Add up 2 and 6 and you get 8, a number some numerology traditions link to upheaval and karmic reckoning. For anyone who already believes in that system, a disaster landing on the 26th isn't a coincidence: it's confirmation. There's no actual link between a calendar date and earthquakes, floods or violence. But belief doesn't need a mechanism. It just needs enough stories that fit, and the 26th has no shortage of those by now.What the 'jinx' really tells usSo what does the list really tell us? Not that the date is cursed; just that disasters don't check the calendar, and over a long enough stretch of history, every date ends up with its own body count. The 26th's list happens to include some of the most consequential disasters of the last century, ones big enough that they changed building codes, early-warning systems, even how countries think about security. That's really why the date sticks in memory. Not the number itself, but what it forced people to rebuild afterward.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Fresh attacks kill four in Ukraine as Kiev targets Russian industry
articles.summary: At least four people were killed and dozens more injured in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, local authorities reported on Saturday, while Ukraine said...
articles.body:
At least four people were killed and dozens injured in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, with residential buildings and industrial targets being hit.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of continuous attacks on towns and villages, resulting in casualties including a five-month-old baby and individuals with limited mobility.

Ukraine retaliated by attacking and damaging industrial targets in Russia, including chemical plants important for the production of tactical and ballistic missiles, as part of its defensive campaign against the ongoing Russian invasion.

At least four people were killed and dozens more injured in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, local authorities reported on Saturday, while Ukraine said it attacked and damaged two industrial targets in Russia.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of attacking towns and villages virtually non-stop.

A drone strike on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia resulted in the death of a woman and a man, he wrote, adding that six people were injured. There were further casualties in an attack on an unnamed company in Zaporizhzhia.

In Odessa on the Black Sea, at least 37 people were injured, according to Zelensky's post. Among those injured was a five-month-old baby.

Images released by the authorities showed a damaged multi-storey residential building.

In Chornomorsk, in the Odessa region, Zelensky wrote that 11 people were injured in a drone attack on a hotel, "including six with limited mobility."

Zelensky: Lack of adequate support from strong powers 'frustrating'

In Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, a missile struck critical infrastructure. Zelensky reported one person had been killed, and three others injured there. Earlier, the governor of the south-eastern Ukrainian region of Dnipropetrovsk, Olexander Hanzha, had reported two deaths and four injuries following an attack on a factory.

Zelensky called on world leaders to do more to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks.

"When the Russians so blatantly turn ordinary people into targets of their terrorist attacks, it is frustrating that the response from the world's strongest powers does not match the level of Russia's escalation," he wrote.

The Defence Ministry in Moscow confirmed the attacks. It said that metal industry companies in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, which manufactured products for military purposes, had been targeted.

In the Odessa region, the targets included port infrastructure and an important facility used for the unloading and storage of military goods, the ministry said. The information cannot be independently verified.

Ukraine claims strikes on Russian industry

Ukraine meanwhile said it had attacked and damaged several targets in Russia, with Zelensky reporting on Facebook on Saturday that long-range drones had struck two chemical plants - one in Togliatti in the south-eastern Samara region and the other in the Perm region in the foothills of the Urals.

A fire was detected on the premises of the plant in Togliatti, the General Staff in Kiev said earlier on Saturday.

The company specializes in the production of synthetic rubbers, which are important for the use of tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the statement.

Early on Saturday, Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a major Ukrainian drone attack on Telegram, without providing details about the target.

The mayor of Togliatti, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person had been taken to hospital following a massive attack on the city. Several multi-storey residential buildings have been damaged, he said.

Unverified images and videos purporting to show a large cloud of smoke in Togliatti were circulating on social media. The city is located around 750 kilometres from Russia's border with Ukraine.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a large-scale Russian invasion for more than four and a half years with Western assistance. As part of its defensive campaign, it repeatedly targets locations deep within Russian territory.

articles.title: At 4, Casey Kloepfer lost his NYPD father on 9/11; 25 years later, he became an NYPD officer, wears his father's badge number and plays for the lacrosse team his father founded
articles.summary: US News: At four years of age, Casey Kloepfer was too young to understand why his father never came home from work. Twenty-five years later, he carries that lo.
articles.body: At four years of age, Casey Kloepfer was too young to understand why his father never came home from work. Twenty-five years later, he carries that loss into the same department his father served, wearing his father's badge number and playing for the NYPD lacrosse team his father helped create, states an online report by NYC Government website. For Casey, the connection to his father is not confined to a photograph, a memorial or a family story. It is woven into the uniform he wears and the department he chose to join.A father lost on September 11Ronnie Kloepfer was an NYPD officer who was killed in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. He was among the thousands of first responders who rushed toward danger as others tried to escape. His death left behind a family that, like so many others, had to navigate life without someone who had been at its center. Ronnie's connection to the NYPD extended beyond his work as a police officer. He was also instrumental in establishing the department's lacrosse team, bringing together officers through a sport he loved and the team would eventually become an unexpected bridge between generations.Following his father's pathA quarter-century after September 11, Casey became an NYPD officer himself. His decision gave a new meaning to a legacy that could easily have remained rooted in the past. He now wears his father's badge number, carrying a small but deeply personal reminder of the man whose career ended before Casey was old enough to understand it.Casey is also part of the same lacrosse tradition his father helped establish. Alongside other officers whose families share similar connections to the department, he keeps alive something that began long before the attacks. The significance is particularly powerful because the NYPD's relationship with September 11 did not end when the World Trade Center towers fell. Hundreds of officers who responded that day and worked at Ground Zero in the months that followed have since died from illnesses linked to their service.A legacy that keeps moving forwardThe story of Casey and his father reflects a larger reality within the NYPD. The department has spent 25 years carrying the memory of those it lost while welcoming new generations who were children, or not yet born, when the attacks happened. For younger officers, September 11 can feel like distant history. For families such as the Kloepfers, it remains personal. Casey's uniform, badge number and place on his father's lacrosse team bring those two eras together. Ronnie's life was cut short on September 11, but the things he built did not disappear with him. His son now serves in the department he once served, and the lacrosse team he helped found continues to bring NYPD officers together.Images Courtesy: Facebook and New York Daily NewsCatch the latest World News and Live updates.
